title: How To Reverse A Bad Class
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Linsin frames the week before holiday break as an ideal reset point for a class that has become disruptive, disrespectful, or chaotic, offering three concrete actions to reverse course upon returning in January. First, reteach the classroom management plan in exhausting, detailed fashion, using modeling for younger students and precise explanation for older ones, so that boundary lines are unmistakably clear. Second, reteach routines with watchmaker-level precision, since routines are described as a direct reflection of classroom health and transfer to behavior, work habits, and academic performance broadly. Third, and most emphatically, follow through without wavering on every expectation taught, since he argues this single element is 'everything' and any hesitation undoes the first two steps. His closing argument is that a poorly behaved class's current behavior is not a fixed trait of who those students are, and that transformation is available to any teacher, regardless of experience or personal characteristics, who commits fully to the three steps.
points: The week before holiday break is framed as the ideal moment to plan a full reset, since returning in January offers a genuine fresh start.
Routines should be retaught with 'watchmaker' precision, since Linsin treats them as a direct reflection of overall classroom health.
Follow-through is singled out as the decisive factor: any wavering, hesitation, or fear undoes the value of reteaching the plan and routines.
The current bad behavior of a class is explicitly framed as not a fixed trait -- transformation is available to any teacher willing to commit fully.
quotes: If this is your class, then the upcoming break is the best time to turn it around. It offers an opportunity to clear the boards and return in January with a new classroom management approach.
It must be taught in exhausting detail. This might include teacher modeling for younger grade levels and pinpoint explanation and in-place demonstration for older students.
Routines are a reflection of the health of your classroom and therefore must be a high priority.
This is it. This is everything. Whatever you expect of your students, and expressly teach, you must require it. There can be no wavering, hesitation, fear, or laziness.
In fact, the stressful and out-of-control class you have now? That’s not who they really are or what they’re capable of becoming. Transformation is possible.
